tracks.title: Beginner: The Fundamentals
tracks.description: Learn the rules, hand rankings, table positions, and basic gameplay mechanics.

lessons.title: The Royal Flush
lessons.content: The highest possible hand in Texas Hold'em. It consists of an Ace, King, Queen, Jack, and 10, all of the same suit. It is practically unbeatable.

lessons.title: Straight Flush
lessons.content: Five cards of sequential rank, all of the same suit. For example: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 of Clubs. The higher the top card, the stronger the straight flush.

lessons.title: Four of a Kind & Full House
lessons.content: Four of a Kind consists of four cards of the same rank (e.g., four Aces). A Full House consists of three cards of one rank and two cards of another rank (e.g., three Kings and two 8s).

lessons.title: Flush & Straight
lessons.content: A Flush is any five cards of the same suit, not in sequence. A Straight is five cards of sequential rank in at least two different suits.

lessons.title: Quiz: Identify the Hand
lessons.question: What hand is currently face down on the table? Click the cards to flip them and find out!

lessons.title: The Button (Dealer)
lessons.content: The Button is the most advantageous position at the table. After the first betting round (pre-flop), the Button acts last on every subsequent round, giving them the most information about other players' actions.

lessons.title: The Blinds (SB & BB)
lessons.content: The two players to the left of the Button are the Small Blind and Big Blind. They must post forced bets before cards are dealt to ensure there is money in the pot to play for.

lessons.title: Early Position (UTG)
lessons.content: Under the Gun (UTG) is the player immediately to the left of the Big Blind. They are the first to act pre-flop. This is the worst position to be in, so you should only play very strong starting hands from here.

lessons.title: Quiz: Best Position
lessons.question: Based on what you just learned, what is considered the best position at the poker table?

lessons.title: Pre-Flop
lessons.content: Every player receives two private 'hole cards'. The first betting round begins, starting with the player to the left of the Big Blind (UTG). Players can Fold, Call (match the Big Blind), or Raise.

lessons.title: The Flop
lessons.content: The dealer places three community cards face up on the board. All remaining players can use these cards to make their hand. A second betting round occurs, starting with the Small Blind.

lessons.title: The Turn
lessons.content: A fourth community card is dealt face up. This is followed by a third betting round.

lessons.title: The River & Showdown
lessons.content: The fifth and final community card is dealt. After the final betting round, if more than one player remains, a 'Showdown' occurs. Players reveal their cards, and the highest five-card hand wins the pot.

lessons.title: Quiz: Community Cards
lessons.question: How many community cards are dealt face-up during 'The Flop'?

lessons.title: Counting Chips & Pot Size
lessons.content: Always keep track of how many chips are in the pot. This determines whether a bet is large or small. A $10 bet into a $20 pot is a half-pot bet, while a $10 bet into a $100 pot is very small.

lessons.title: Quiz: Pot Sizing
lessons.question: If the pot is $50 and you bet $25, what fraction of the pot did you bet?

lessons.title: Basic Table Etiquette
lessons.content: Good etiquette keeps the game fun and fair. Always act in turn. Do not discuss your folded cards while a hand is still being played, as it can influence the action. Keep your cards visible to the dealer and other players at all times.

lessons.title: Physical & Timing Tells
lessons.content: A 'tell' is a clue a player gives about the strength of their hand. Physical tells include shaking hands or staring at chips. In online poker, 'timing tells' (how fast someone acts) are very common. A fast call often indicates a draw or marginal hand, while a long tank followed by a big raise usually means immense strength.

lessons.title: Texas Hold'em vs Omaha
lessons.content: While Texas Hold'em (2 hole cards) is the most popular variant, Pot Limit Omaha (PLO) is another major game where you receive 4 hole cards but MUST use exactly 2 of them to make your hand.

lessons.title: Limit vs. No-Limit
lessons.content: In No-Limit games, you can bet all your chips at any time. In Limit games, bet sizes are fixed (e.g., $2 on the flop, $4 on the turn), making it a much more mathematical and less psychological game.

lessons.title: Common Poker Terms
lessons.content: Poker has its own language. The 'Nuts' means the best possible hand. A 'Bad Beat' is when a heavily favored hand loses to a lucky draw. Being 'In the Money' (ITM) means you have survived long enough in a tournament to guarantee a payout.

lessons.title: Board Textures
lessons.content: A 'Dry' board (like 2-7-K of different suits) has few draw possibilities. A 'Wet' board (like 8-9-10 with two hearts) is very dangerous because it offers many straight and flush draws.

tracks.title: Intermediate: Strategy & Odds
tracks.description: Master pot odds, starting hand selection, and betting strategies.

lessons.title: Understanding Pot Odds
lessons.content: Pot odds represent the ratio between the size of the pot and the size of the bet you face. For example, if the pot is $100 and you need to call $50, your pot odds are 2-to-1. You must win at least 33% of the time to make this a profitable call.

lessons.title: Outs and Equity
lessons.content: An 'out' is a card that will improve your hand to a winning one. You can estimate your equity (chance of winning) using the Rule of 4 and 2: Multiply your outs by 4 on the flop, or by 2 on the turn, to get your approximate percentage chance of hitting your card.

lessons.title: Quiz: The Rule of 4
lessons.question: You have a flush draw (9 outs) on the flop. Using the Rule of 4, what is your approximate chance of hitting your flush by the river?

lessons.title: Premium Hands
lessons.content: Premium hands include big pocket pairs (AA, KK, QQ) and strong connectors (AK). These hands should almost always be raised pre-flop to build the pot and thin the field.

lessons.title: Speculative Hands
lessons.content: Speculative hands like suited connectors (e.g., 8-9 suited) or small pocket pairs rely on hitting a strong flop (like a straight, flush, or set). They play best in late position and multi-way pots where the implied odds are high.

lessons.title: Quiz: Premium vs Speculative
lessons.question: Which of the following is considered a 'Premium' starting hand that you should raise aggressively pre-flop?

lessons.title: Value Betting
lessons.content: A value bet is made when you believe you have the best hand, and you want a worse hand to call. The goal is to maximize the amount of money you extract from your opponent without betting so much that they fold.

lessons.title: Effective Bluffing
lessons.content: Bluffing is betting with a weak hand to force better hands to fold. The most effective bluffs tell a believable story across multiple betting rounds and target opponents who are capable of folding.

lessons.title: Quiz: Value or Bluff?
lessons.question: If you bet on the river with the absolute best possible hand (the 'nuts'), what type of bet are you making?

lessons.title: Playing In Position (IP)
lessons.content: Playing 'in position' means you act after your opponent on each betting round. This gives you complete information about their actions before you have to make yours, allowing you to control the size of the pot.

lessons.title: Playing Out of Position (OOP)
lessons.content: Playing 'out of position' means acting first. You must play much stronger hands OOP because you lack information. It is harder to extract value and easier to get bluffed.

lessons.title: Bankroll Management (BRM)
lessons.content: Your bankroll is your poker lifeblood. A standard rule is to have at least 20 to 30 buy-ins for cash games, and 100 buy-ins for tournaments. Practicing good BRM ensures you can survive the natural mathematical variance (downswings) of the game without going broke.

lessons.title: Understanding Tilt
lessons.content: 'Tilt' is a state of mental or emotional confusion where a player adopts a less than optimal strategy, usually resulting in the player becoming overly aggressive. Recognizing when you are on tilt and taking a break is one of the most profitable skills you can develop.

lessons.title: Quiz: Bankroll Safety
lessons.question: If you have a total poker bankroll of $1,000, what is the maximum buy-in cash game you should play to adhere to a conservative 20 buy-in rule?

lessons.title: Cash Game Dynamics
lessons.content: In cash games, chips represent real money, and you can rebuy at any time. The blinds stay the same, allowing you to patiently wait for good hands. The goal is long-term profit.

lessons.title: Tournament Dynamics
lessons.content: In tournaments, you pay a fixed entry fee for a starting stack. Blinds constantly increase, forcing action. Survival is key, and you cannot rebuy once you lose your chips (unless it's a specific rebuy tournament).

lessons.title: Why Multi-table?
lessons.content: Online poker allows you to play multiple tables at once. This increases your hourly win rate by allowing you to play more hands per hour, smoothing out variance faster. However, your edge per table decreases as your attention is divided.

lessons.title: Tiling vs Stacking
lessons.content: 'Tiling' means arranging tables side-by-side so you can see all action. 'Stacking' means putting all tables on top of each other, where the table requiring action pops to the front. Start with 2-4 tiled tables before trying to stack.

tracks.title: Advanced: GTO & Exploitative Play
tracks.description: Learn Game Theory Optimal (GTO) concepts and how to exploit opponent tendencies.

lessons.title: What is GTO?
lessons.content: Game Theory Optimal (GTO) poker involves playing a balanced, mathematically sound strategy that makes you unexploitable by your opponents. By balancing your value bets and bluffs perfectly, your opponents' decisions become indifferent.

lessons.title: Exploitative Play
lessons.content: While GTO makes you unexploitable, maximum profit often comes from Exploitative play—deviating from GTO to take advantage of specific weaknesses in your opponents' strategies, such as over-folding or calling too much.

lessons.title: The Art of the 3-Bet
lessons.content: A 3-bet is the second raise pre-flop (the big blind is the 1st bet, an open raise is the 2nd, and the re-raise is the 3-bet). A polarized 3-betting range includes your absolute best hands (AA, KK) and some bluffs (like A5 suited).

lessons.title: Continuation Betting (C-Bet)
lessons.content: A continuation bet is made on the flop by the pre-flop aggressor. A GTO c-betting strategy considers range advantage. If the flop heavily favors the pre-flop raiser's range (e.g., A-K-2), they should c-bet frequently.

lessons.title: What is ICM?
lessons.content: The Independent Chip Model (ICM) applies to tournaments. It assigns a real-dollar value to your tournament chips based on the payout structure. Under ICM, chips lost are worth more than chips gained, meaning you must play tighter near the money bubble.

lessons.title: Push/Fold Charts
lessons.content: When your stack drops below 15 Big Blinds in a tournament, you should generally only go all-in or fold pre-flop. Memorizing push/fold Nash Equilibrium charts is essential for late-stage tournament success.

lessons.title: Thinking in Ranges
lessons.content: Amateurs put their opponents on a specific hand (e.g., 'He has Ace-King'). Professionals put their opponents on a 'range' of possible hands based on their actions, position, and player type. You then compare how your specific hand performs against their entire range.

lessons.title: Using Blockers
lessons.content: A 'blocker' is a card in your hand that makes it impossible (or less likely) for your opponent to have a specific hand. For example, if you hold the Ace of Spades, you 'block' your opponent from having the nut flush in spades. Blockers are heavily used in advanced bluffing and calling strategies.

lessons.title: HUDs and Tracking Software
lessons.content: Heads-Up Displays (HUDs) overlay statistics on your opponents in real-time (like VPIP and PFR). Tracking software databases your hands, allowing you to review your play and plug leaks in your strategy.

lessons.title: Poker Solvers (PIO/GTO+)
lessons.content: A solver is a program that calculates Game Theory Optimal (GTO) strategies for specific poker situations. Advanced players spend hundreds of hours studying solver outputs to understand complex river bluffs and range balancing.

lessons.title: The Metagame
lessons.content: The 'Metagame' refers to the game outside the game. When playing against the same regulars (regs) repeatedly, your past actions influence their future decisions. You might intentionally play a hand sub-optimally to set up a massive bluff in a future session.

lessons.title: Table Selection (Bumhunting)
lessons.content: In high stakes cash games, table selection is paramount. 'Bumhunting' refers to the practice of only sitting at tables with a known recreational player (a 'fish'). If a table is entirely composed of strong professionals, the only winner is the casino collecting the rake.
